concepts.name: What This Program Is Not
concepts.definition: Finishing the program shows you understand the material. It does not mean you have a profitable strategy.

concepts.name: Market Time And Your Time
concepts.definition: Markets keep the clock of the place they are in. Your clock may differ, and the difference can change during the year.

concepts.name: The Analyst's Frame
concepts.definition: Eight questions that turn a hunch into a reasoned decision.

concepts.name: Decimals
concepts.definition: Reading and subtracting decimal numbers.

concepts.name: Percentages
concepts.definition: Finding a percent of a number and a percent change.

concepts.name: Ratios
concepts.definition: Reading a ratio such as 1:3.

concepts.name: Negative Numbers
concepts.definition: Adding and multiplying with gains and losses.

concepts.name: What Trading Is
concepts.definition: Buying or selling something to profit from a change in its price, over a short or medium time.

concepts.name: The Parts Of A Trade
concepts.definition: Every trade has a market, a direction, a size, an entry, an exit and a risk limit.

concepts.name: Trading Versus Investing
concepts.definition: Investors hold for growth and income over years. Traders aim to profit from price moves over a shorter time. Both can lose money.

concepts.name: Trading Versus Gambling
concepts.definition: Both involve uncertainty. In trading you choose and cap your risk, and a measured edge is possible. Acting on a hunch with no plan is gambling in any market.

concepts.name: Costs Work Against You
concepts.definition: Every trade has a cost. Your average trade must beat it before it earns anything.

concepts.name: Why Markets Exist
concepts.definition: Markets let people exchange, discover prices, raise money and pass on risk.

concepts.name: Who Trades
concepts.definition: Central banks, banks, companies, funds, individuals and automated firms trade for different reasons. Most are not trying to profit from short price moves.

concepts.name: What Moves A Price
concepts.definition: A price is where a buyer and a seller last agreed. More buying than selling pushes it up, and the reverse pushes it down.

concepts.name: Stories After The Fact
concepts.definition: A neat explanation of a move that already happened is not a prediction of the next one.

concepts.name: What An Edge Is
concepts.definition: An edge is an average gain per trade, after costs, that is supported by evidence.

concepts.name: Expected Value
concepts.definition: The average result of a bet if it were repeated many times: multiply each outcome by its chance, then add.

concepts.name: Edge Versus Belief
concepts.definition: A belief is a feeling that something will happen. An edge is a measured average over many recorded trades.

concepts.name: Probability As Frequency
concepts.definition: A 60% chance means about 6 in 10 over many tries. It says nothing certain about the next one.

concepts.name: One Result Versus Many
concepts.definition: One result cannot be predicted. The spread of many results can.

concepts.name: Independent Results
concepts.definition: When results are independent, the last result does not change the chance of the next.

concepts.name: Losing Streaks
concepts.definition: Runs of losses happen in any random sequence, including inside a strategy that wins on average.

concepts.name: Luck Makes Results Differ
concepts.definition: Traders with identical rules and identical odds still get very different results because of luck.

concepts.name: Process Versus Outcome
concepts.definition: A decision is judged by the plan and information behind it. The result is a separate question.

concepts.name: A Good Trade Versus A Profitable One
concepts.definition: A good trade follows a tested plan at acceptable risk. It can still lose. A poor trade can win by luck.

concepts.name: The Pip
concepts.definition: The standard step in which a currency price is measured: 0.0001 on most pairs, 0.01 on yen pairs.

concepts.name: Lots
concepts.definition: A standard lot is 100,000 units of the first currency in the pair.

concepts.name: Pip Value
concepts.definition: What one pip is worth in your account currency for your position size.

jpy-pip-100x.label: using 0.0001 as the pip size on a yen pair
jpy-pip-100x.fix: On yen pairs a pip is 0.01, not 0.0001.

pip-pipette-10x.label: treating a pipette as a pip
pip-pipette-10x.fix: A pip is ten pipettes. The fifth decimal (third on yen pairs) is the pipette.

no-conversion.label: forgetting to convert into the account currency
no-conversion.fix: Pip value first comes out in the pair's second currency. Convert it to your account currency.

per-lot-only.label: giving the value for one lot, not the whole trade
per-lot-only.fix: Multiply the per-lot value by the number of lots.

wrong-way-conversion.label: converting with the rate the wrong way round
wrong-way-conversion.fix: Divide by the pair price when the account currency is the first currency in the pair.

sign-error.label: getting the sign wrong on a gain or a loss
sign-error.fix: A loss is negative. A profit is positive.

percent-as-decimal.label: mixing up a percent and a decimal
percent-as-decimal.fix: 0.5% is 0.005 as a decimal. Divide a percent by 100.

ev-forgot-probability.label: adding the outcomes without weighting them by their chances
ev-forgot-probability.fix: Multiply each outcome by its probability, then add.

confuse-win-loss.label: giving the number of losses when the wins were asked for
confuse-win-loss.fix: Read the question again: which side is being asked for?

added-not-multiplied.label: adding chances that should be multiplied
added-not-multiplied.fix: For independent results in a row, multiply the chances.

outcome-bias.label: judging a decision by its result
outcome-bias.fix: Judge the decision by the information and plan you had, not by how it turned out.

gamblers-fallacy.label: believing a win is "due" after losses
gamblers-fallacy.fix: Independent outcomes do not remember the past. A run of losses does not make a win more likely.

small-sample.label: drawing a conclusion from a handful of results
small-sample.fix: A few results can be luck. An edge shows only over many trades.

hindsight-story.label: treating an after-the-fact story as a prediction
hindsight-story.fix: A neat explanation of a move that already happened does not tell you what happens next.

win-rate-is-edge.label: treating a high win rate as the same as an edge
win-rate-is-edge.fix: Edge depends on how much you win and lose, not only how often. Multiply and add.

ignoring-costs.label: forgetting that every trade has a cost
ignoring-costs.fix: Spreads and fees are paid every time. Your average trade has to beat them.

belief-as-edge.label: treating a feeling or a story as an edge
belief-as-edge.fix: An edge is a measured average over many recorded trades, not a conviction.

trading-as-gambling.label: acting on luck or a hunch with no plan or limit
trading-as-gambling.fix: A plan with a fixed risk is what separates a trade from a bet.

certainty-thinking.label: expecting a certain result from a single trade
certainty-thinking.fix: A single trade is one draw from a range of possible outcomes.

profit-means-good.label: assuming a profit means the decision was good
profit-means-good.fix: A rule-breaking trade can win by luck. Check the process first.

loss-means-bad.label: assuming a loss means the decision was bad
loss-means-bad.fix: A well-planned trade can lose. Losses are part of any edge.

lessons.title: How This Program Works
lessons.aim: Know how the lessons, levels, ranks and daily Warm-Up fit together.

blocks.text: Each lesson is short. You read a little, try something, then answer a few questions. This is the cycle: **understand**, **practice**, **test**, **demonstrate**, **advance**.
The program has 13 levels. Each one ends with an assessment. Pass it and the next level opens.
As you pass levels you earn ranks, from Beginner up to Apprentice. A rank shows what you have learned. It does not show that you can make money.
Each day the app asks about ten questions from earlier lessons. It takes about five minutes.
Old material comes back on purpose. Knowing something today does not mean you will know it next month.
Your mentor marks your written answers and can help when you are stuck. Written answers are marked by a person, not by the app.

lessons.title: Set Your Clocks
lessons.aim: Set your time zone and read market time against your own.

blocks.text: Markets keep the time of the place they are in. London trades on London time. New York trades on New York time. Your own clock is a third clock.
This app always shows **market time** and **your time**, each with its zone beside it.
Guyana is four hours behind UTC all year. It never changes its clocks.
Many countries do change theirs, in spring and autumn, and not on the same dates.
For a few weeks a year the US and the UK are on different clock offsets, so the gap between New York and London is four hours instead of five.
Your clock does not move, so the times markets open shift on your clock. Later lessons train you to convert these correctly.

lessons.title: The Analyst's Frame
lessons.aim: Use eight questions to turn a hunch into a reasoned decision.

blocks.text: This program never asks "what is the right trade?" It asks you to think. These eight questions are how.

items: What information do I have?
What are the possible outcomes?
What would show my idea is wrong?
What is my risk?
What does the evidence say?
Is there actually an edge?
How large is my sample?
Could this result be random?

blocks.text: Decide whether to carry an umbrella to work. Look at the sky, the forecast and your past experience. Then answer the eight questions in your own words.

You will use the same eight questions on trades, on test results and on your own journal.

The hints fade as you get better.

lessons.title: What Is Trading?
lessons.aim: Say what trading is and name the parts of every trade.

blocks.text: Trading is buying or selling something to profit from a change in its price, over a short or medium time.
You are not trying to own it for life. You are trying to profit from the price moving.
Every trade has the same six parts.

items: **Market:** what you trade.
**Direction:** buy or sell.
**Size:** how much.
**Entry:** the price where you start.
**Exit:** the price where you finish.
**Risk limit:** the most you will lose, set before you start.

blocks.text: You enter, you hold, you exit. While a trade is open its profit or loss keeps changing.
It only becomes final when you exit.

blocks.title: Buy, hold, sell
steps: You buy 10 units at $50. You spend $500.
You sell all 10 at $53. You receive $530.

blocks.text: You can also sell first and buy back later if you expect a fall. That comes in Level 3.

lessons.title: Trading Versus Investing
lessons.aim: Tell trading and investing apart and say why neither is safe or easy.

blocks.text: **Investing** means buying something to own for a long time. The return comes from growth and income, such as company profits or interest, as well as price changes.
**Trading** means aiming to profit from price moves over a shorter time. You decide more often.

items: **Time held:** years for an investor. Minutes to weeks for a trader.
**Where the return comes from:** growth and income for an investor. Price moves for a trader.
**How often you decide:** rarely for an investor. Often for a trader.
**Costs:** they matter to both, and more the more often you trade.

blocks.title: Neither Is Safe Or Easy
blocks.text: Investing is not automatically safe. Trading is not fast money. Either can lose.
Some people hold for months and call it trading. Some trade every day and call it investing.
What matters is what you are doing and why: your time frame, your reason and your plan.

Neither is safe. Neither is easy.

lessons.title: Trading Versus Gambling
lessons.aim: Explain what trading and gambling share and what can set them apart.

blocks.text: In both you do not know what happens next. The uncertainty is the same.

items: In a game like roulette, the payouts are set so the house wins on average. That built-in advantage is the **house edge**. You cannot change it.
In trading, nobody sets the odds against you. You choose what to trade, when, and how much to risk.
In trading you can record your results over many trades and check whether you have an advantage. Lesson 1.07 shows how.

blocks.text: Every trade has a cost, such as the gap between the buy price and the sell price. It is small, but you pay it each time.
Your average trade has to beat those costs before it earns anything.

blocks.text: Trading does not pay just because it is not a casino. This program teaches you to measure whether you have an edge. It does not tell you that you will.
The **expected value** of a bet is its average result if you could repeat it many times. Multiply each result by its chance, then add.

lessons.title: Why Financial Markets Exist
lessons.aim: Explain the jobs a market does and where a trader fits.

steps.title: A Market Is A Meeting Place

blocks.text: A market is where buyers and sellers meet and agree a price. It can be a place or a screen.

items: **Exchange:** people swap one thing for another, such as one currency for another.
**Set prices:** buyers and sellers together show what something is worth right now.
**Raise money:** a company can sell shares to fund a project.
**Pass on risk:** someone can pay to avoid a price change that would hurt them.

blocks.title: An importer
steps: An importer must pay a foreign supplier in US dollars next month.
The importer worries the exchange rate will move against them.
A market lets them agree a rate now, which protects them from the move.

blocks.text: The importer is not trying to profit from the rate. They want certainty.
Markets did not appear so that people could trade for profit. Traders are one kind of participant among many, and they are on the other side of trades made for other reasons.

exercise.explanation: Each example is a different job that a market does.

points: A market is where buyers and sellers agree prices.
Markets let people exchange, set prices, raise money and pass on risk.
Traders are one kind of participant, not the reason markets exist.

lessons.title: Who Participates In Markets?
lessons.aim: Name the main kinds of participants and their different motives.

items: **Central banks:** manage a country's money and interest rates.
**Banks and dealers:** buy and sell for customers and for themselves.
**Companies:** exchange money to pay suppliers and receive customers' payments.
**Funds:** manage pooled money for many people.
**Individual traders:** people trading their own money, like you.
**Automated firms:** computers that follow rules and trade very fast.

steps.title: Not Everyone Wants A Profit From The Price

blocks.text: A company paying a supplier is not speculating. A central bank follows policy goals. A fund follows its own rules. Each has its own reason to buy or sell.
An individual trader is a very small participant. Your orders will not move the price.
You will be trading against people and firms with more information and better tools. That is why measuring an edge matters so much.
A big order made for a non-trading reason, such as paying a supplier, can move a price without carrying any message about the future. You cannot see anyone's motive from the price alone.

points: Central banks, banks, companies, funds, individuals and automated firms all trade.

An individual is a very small participant.

lessons.title: Why Do Prices Move?
lessons.aim: Explain a price move as buying against selling, and say why after-the-fact stories are not predictions.

steps.title: A Price Is Where A Trade Happened

blocks.text: The price is the level at which a buyer and a seller last agreed to trade.
When more people want to buy than sell, buyers must pay more to get filled. The price rises.
When more want to sell than buy, sellers must accept less. The price falls.

items: New information, such as a news release.
Changed expectations about the future.
Needs that have nothing to do with the price, such as paying a bill.
Large players changing their positions.

blocks.text: After a move, people explain it with a tidy story about the news.
In real time the cause is often unclear, and several forces act at once. A story that explains a move that already happened is **hindsight**. It is not a forecast.

steps.title: Buying Against Selling
steps.intro: First choose what you expect. Then run it.

points: A price is where a buyer and seller last agreed.
More buying than selling pushes it up. More selling pushes it down.
Many forces act at once, and the cause is often unclear in real time.
A story after the fact is not a prediction.

lessons.title: What Is An Edge?
lessons.aim: Define an edge and tell it apart from a belief.

blocks.text: An edge is an average gain per trade, after costs, that is supported by evidence.
An edge is not a property of one trade. It is what happens on average across many.
A trade can lose while the method still has an edge. A trade can win with no edge at all.

blocks.title: Two statements
steps: **Edge:** "Across 300 recorded trades, this method averaged +$4 per trade after costs."

blocks.text: The first is a feeling. The second is a measurement. (The numbers here are an illustration, not a real result.)
Real edges are small. Even a real edge produces runs of losses. A small edge takes many trades to show up.
That is why a few good results prove nothing. Level 13 shows you how to measure this properly.
Expected value is the tool for asking "does this bet pay on average?" A positive expected value, after costs, is what an edge looks like in numbers.
A high win rate is not the same thing. It depends how much you win and lose too. You will see this in Level 5.

steps.title: Two Coins
steps.intro: One coin lands heads 50% of the time. The other, 52%. Can you tell which is which?

steps.title: Another Expected Value
steps.intro: Use the − key for a negative number.

points: An edge is a measured average gain per trade after costs.
A belief is a feeling. An edge is evidence.
A real edge is small and noisy, and needs many trades to show.
A high win rate is not the same as an edge.

lessons.title: Probability And Uncertainty
lessons.aim: Explain why one result cannot be predicted but many results can.

blocks.text: A 60% chance means about 6 in 10 over many tries. It says nothing certain about the next one.
You cannot predict one coin flip. But 100 flips will land close to 50 heads.
One result is unpredictable. The spread of many results is predictable.
For this lesson, treat each trade as its own draw, and do not let the last result change your view of the next. Results like this are called **independent**.

steps.title: A Loss Streak Does Not Make A Win Due

blocks.text: After four losses in a row, the fifth is not "due" to win. The market has no memory of your results. This mistake has a name, the **gambler's fallacy**. You will meet it again in Level 11.

steps.title: The Probability Lab
steps.intro: Choose a win rate and a number of trades. Predict first. Then run 1,000 tries.

points: Probability is how often something happens over many tries.
One result cannot be predicted. The spread of many can.
Independent results do not remember the past.
A loss streak does not make a win due.

lessons.title: Why Traders Experience Losing Streaks
lessons.aim: Show with a simulation that runs of losses are normal, even for a method that wins on average.

blocks.text: Flip a fair coin 100 times and you will see runs of heads and runs of tails. Nothing is wrong with the coin. Random results just cluster.

steps.title: A Winning Method Still Has Losing Runs

blocks.text: Even a method that wins 6 times in 10 will have several losses in a row now and then. A losing run does not mean the method has stopped working.
The lower the win rate, the longer the losing runs tend to be. Some good methods win less than half the time.
Give twenty traders the same rules and the same odds. Their results will still look very different, because of luck.
That is why one person's good or bad run tells you little about their skill.

steps.title: The Streak Simulator
steps.intro: Choose a win rate. Predict the longest losing streak. Then run twenty identical traders.

points: Random results come in runs.
A method that wins on average still has losing runs.
Lower win rates make longer losing runs.
Traders with identical rules get different results from luck alone.

lessons.title: A Good Trade Versus A Profitable Trade
lessons.aim: Judge a decision by its quality, separately from its result.

blocks.text: Was the decision good? And did it make money? They are different questions.
A good decision can lose. A poor decision can win. Neither result changes the quality of the decision.

items: It followed a plan that was tested.
Risk stayed within the limit.
It used only the information available at the time.

blocks.text: If you judge by results, you learn the wrong lessons. You keep habits that got lucky, and you drop good ones that lost. Over time that costs you.

steps.title: Sort Twelve Decisions
steps.intro: Tap a decision, then tap the box where it belongs.

exercise.prompt: Each trader made a decision. Sort them by the quality of the decision and the result.

items.text: Followed every rule in the plan. The trade made money.
Followed every rule in the plan. The trade lost.
Ignored the plan and traded on a hunch. It made money.
Ignored the plan and doubled the size. It lost.
Waited for the setup, risked the planned amount, and lost.
Skipped the trade because the plan said there was no setup. The price then rose.
Entered late out of excitement, with no limit. It made money.
Moved the risk limit further away to avoid a loss. It lost more.
Traded the planned size with the limit in place. It made money.
Took a large risk on a tip. It lost.
Sat out a news release because the plan says to. The price jumped.
Traded without checking the plan, and the trade paid off.

itemFeedback.i1: Following the plan was right. A loss is part of any method.
itemFeedback.i2: The win was luck. The decision was still poor.
itemFeedback.i5: The plan said no. The price rising afterwards does not make the decision poor.

exercise.explanation: Judge the decision first. The result is a separate question.

steps.title: In Your Own Words
steps.prompt: Why can a trader have a losing trade while following a method that is profitable on average? Write a few sentences.
steps.modelAnswer: Each trade is only one draw from a range of possible results. A method that wins on average still loses some of its trades, and even runs of them, because results vary. So one loss does not show the method is broken, and one win does not show it is good. You judge the method over many trades and you judge each decision by whether it followed the plan.
rubric: Each trade is one draw from a range of outcomes.
An edge shows over many trades, not one.
Losing trades are an expected part of a profitable method.
Judge the decision by process, not by one result.
Small samples can mislead in either direction.

points: Decision quality and result are separate questions.
A good decision can lose. A poor decision can win.
Judging by results teaches the wrong lessons.
A good decision follows a tested plan at acceptable risk.

lessons.title: Pip Value
lessons.aim: Work out what one pip is worth in your account currency.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text: This lesson is from Level 3. The lessons before it are not built yet, so here are the two ideas you need.
A **pip** is the standard step of a currency price: 0.0001 on most pairs, and 0.01 on yen pairs.
A **lot** is a position size. One standard lot is 100,000 units of the first currency.
**Pip value** is what one pip is worth in money for your position, in your account currency.
It depends on three things:

items: The pip size of the pair.
The size of your position, in lots.
The second currency in the pair, compared with your account currency.

blocks.text: Trade EUR/USD with a US-dollar account. The second currency is already dollars.
Half a lot is $5 per pip. Two lots is $20 per pip.

steps.title: Case Two: Convert To Your Currency

blocks.text: When the second currency is not your account currency, the pip value first comes out in that currency. Then you convert it.

blocks.title: USD/JPY at 150, one lot
steps: Yen pair, so the pip size is 0.01.
One dollar buys 150 yen, so 1,000 yen is 1,000 ÷ 150 = **$6.67**.

blocks.text: Ask one question: how many dollars is one unit of that second currency worth?

items: **Yen:** one yen is 1 ÷ 150 dollars, so **divide** by the USD/JPY price.
**Canadian dollars:** one is 1 ÷ 1.36 dollars, so **divide** by the USD/CAD price.
**Pounds:** one pound is 1.35 dollars, so **multiply** by the GBP/USD price.

blocks.title: The Yen Trap
blocks.text: On a yen pair the pip is 0.01, not 0.0001. Using the wrong one makes your answer 100 times too small.

blocks.title: USD/JPY at 150, half a lot, dollar account
steps: In dollars: 1,000 ÷ 150 = $6.67 per pip for one lot.

steps.title: Guided Calculator
steps.intro: Fill in each step. If one step is off, the next steps are still marked against your own number.

steps.title: Use The Calculator
steps.intro: Try different pairs and lot sizes. Open Show Working to see each step.

points: Pip value depends on pip size, lots, and the second currency.
Second currency = your account currency: nothing to convert.
Otherwise, convert. Divide when dollars are the first currency, multiply when dollars are the second.
Yen pairs use a 0.01 pip.
